detail.text: What is left is exactly the integral points of one elliptic curve, 1611.a1: the LMFDB computes them from a Mordell–Weil basis with an elliptic-logarithm bound (Stroeker–Tzanakis 1994; Sage/Magma IntegralPoints). Mathlib has neither Mordell–Weil for a specific curve nor a Baker-type lower bound for linear forms in elliptic logarithms, so the hole is not formalisable today and is not split further: any split would be a restatement. route.text: Reduce the pair equation to integral points on the minimal model of the elliptic curve 1611.a1 (y^2 + y = x^3 - 9x + 20) by x = 3(m-1), y = 9n - 5; partial PR #1168 proves the map and reads the binomial solutions off the curve's integral points, one hole = that list.

literature_proposed.summary: Known. The pair (2,3): Avanesov (1966) determined every integer solution of C(n,2) = C(m,3) (an elliptic curve); in the half triangle they are (16,10), (56,22), (120,36), values 120, 1540, 7140. Not formalised; a formalisation needs integral points on an elliptic curve.

review.words: Is it true that, for every integer $t\geq1$, there is some integer $a$ such that ${n \choose k} = a$ with $1\leq k \le \frac{n}{2}$ has exactly $t$ solutions?
